Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Consumers Commission publishes third annual Gambling Survey for Great Britain 16 July 2026 The Gambling Commission has today published the third annual report from the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB). The survey has provided three consecutive years of official statistics from 2023 to 2025 on gambling participation, behaviours, attitudes and consequences across Great Britain. Produced by the National Centre for Social Research and the University of Glasgow, GSGB is one of the world's largest dedicated gambling surveys, with around 20,000 respondents each year. Its methodology has been independently reviewed and provides the most comprehensive picture currently available of consumers’ views of their gambling, including the National Lottery, in Great Britain. The survey enables robust trend analysis, allowing the Commission and external stakeholders to identify patterns, track changes over time and develop a deeper understanding of how gambling participation and experiences are evolving. Key findings from this year's report include: headline participation rates are stable. In 2025, 47 percent of participants aged 18 and over told us they participated in any form of gambling in the past four weeks (27 percent excluding lottery draws only players) the most common reasons for adults to participate in gambling were, for the chance of winning big money (84 percent), because gambling is fun (69 percent), to make money (57 percent) and because it was exciting (53 percent) the level of the population reporting a PGSI score of 8 or more is stable over the three years (2.4 percent in 2025) the majority of gamblers have a positive or neutral feeling towards their gambling. When asked to rate their feelings towards gambling 78 percent had a positive or neutral view. Tim Miller, Executive Director for Research and Policy, Gambling Commission, said: "The publication of the third annual Gambling Survey for Great Britain marks an important milestone. “Three years of GSGB provides a richer, more timely picture of the trend in gambling in Great Britain than has previously been available. It helps us understand not only who gambles and the products they use, but also why people gamble, the range of experiences they have, and the consequences gambling can have in people's lives. This evidence is a vital part of a wider evidence base that informs policy, regulation and wider public discussion. “We encourage researchers, policymakers, industry and the wider public to make use of these findings alongside the interactive dashboard and supplementary reports. As with all official statistics, we remain committed to ensuring GSGB continues to meet the highest standards through transparency, independent scrutiny and ongoing methodological improvement." Note to editors The Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB) is the official statistics publication on gambling in Great Britain. The survey is designed to be used alongside other evidence sources to provide the most comprehensive picture of gambling participation and behaviour. While the wider evidence landscape remains important, direct comparisons between GSGB and surveys using different methodologies are not appropriate. The correct comparison is between successive waves of GSGB, which now provide three-years of consistent, comparable trend data. The survey is conducted by the National Centre for Social Research in partnership with the University of Glasgow. Approximately 20,000 adults aged 18 and over are interviewed each year, making it one of the world's largest dedicated gambling surveys. The publication of the 2025 annual report provides three consecutive years of comparable data, enabling robust trend analysis for the first time. The GSGB is a nationally representative survey producing estimates of gambling behaviours amongst the population and as with any methodology has its own strengths and weaknesses. You can access a full technical report which sets out more detail about these strengths and weaknesses, including the risk of over estimation and under estimation of survey estimates. The interactive Power BI dashboard (opens in new tab) has been updated to include all three years of GSGB data. Two supplementary reports exploring gambling-related consequences have been published alongside the annual report. Additional supplementary reports based on GSGB data will be published throughout the year. Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) ‘Problem gambling’ means gambling to a degree that compromises, disrupts or damages family, personal or recreational pursuits. We currently measure problem gambling prevalence rates via a number of screening tools including the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). This screen measures the following: PGSI score of 8 and over represents problem gambling by which a person will have experienced adverse consequences from gambling and may have lost control of their behaviour. Involvement in gambling can be at any level, but it is likely to be heavy PGSI score of 3 to 7 represents moderate risk gambling by which a person may or may not have experienced any adverse consequences from gambling but may be at risk if they are heavily involved in gambling PGSI score of 1 to 2 represents low risk gambling by which a person is unlikely to have experienced any adverse consequences from gambling but may be at risk if they are heavily involved in gambling. More information about the PGSI screen can be found here Problem gambling screens. For all media enquiries, please contact the Gambling Commission press office . Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Evolution Malta Holding Limited to pay £4.75m 23 July 2026 The Gambling Commission has published a public statement setting out how a software and casino game host licence holder supplied online games to unlicensed gambling businesses. Evolution Malta Holding Limited will pay a £4.75 million settlement after a Commission investigation revealed its games appeared on six unlicensed websites accessible to consumers in Great Britain (GB). During the investigation it was established that Evolution’s risk assessment of whether their business could be used for money laundering and terrorist financing was not effective enough to flag that two operators it conducted business with were supplying its games to consumers in Great Britain without holding a Commission licence. Between December 2023 and November 2024 there were large volumes of visits to the six websites by UK consumers. Evolution breached regulations by not taking appropriate steps to identify and assess the risks of money laundering and terrorist financing, not establishing and maintaining effective policies, procedure and controls needed to ensure that its games were not made available in the GB market by unlicensed operators, and not complying with customer due diligence requirements. John Pierce, Commission Director of Enforcement, said: "This case exposed serious weaknesses in Evolution's money laundering risk assessment and its oversight of risks within its supply chain. "The company's money laundering risk assessment was outdated and failed to adequately consider the risk of its games being made available through unlicensed operators. As a result, there was a significant gap between the controls on paper and their effectiveness in practice. "The Commission's investigation and testing uncovered failings that were serious enough for us to consider licence suspension. "Evolution responded swiftly and comprehensively once these issues were identified, taking immediate action to strengthen its controls and address our concerns. Our subsequent testing has not identified any further instances of concern. “However, this case provides an important lesson for the industry. Operators must ensure their risk assessments are current, regularly tested and reflective of real-world risks. Our priority remains to continue regulating The National Lottery for the benefit of participants and Good Causes." The National Lottery is one of the world’s largest lotteries and since launching in 1994, National Lottery players have collectively raised more than £53 billion for more than 680,000 Good Causes across the UK, transforming lives and contributing to the arts, sport, heritage and communities. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Commission supports police action targeting illegal gambling activity 10 August 2026 The Gambling Commission has supported South Yorkshire Police in a coordinated operation targeting illegal gambling and suspected organised criminal activity in Sheffield and Doncaster. The action, carried out on 4 and 5 August as part of Operation Duxford and Operation Snaresbrook, saw officers execute warrants at venues suspected of involvement in illegal gambling and money laundering. The operation brought together the Gambling Commission, South Yorkshire Police, the Yorkshire & Humber Regional Organised Crime Unit, local authorities and Immigration Enforcement. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Holland Park Leisure Limited fined £150,000 18 August 2026 An Adult Gaming Centre operator is to pay a £150,000 fine for failing to comply with a self-exclusion requirement designed to reduce gambling harm. Holland Park Leisure Limited, which runs three Adult Gaming Centres in Leicester , will also undergo a third-party audit to review the Licensee's policies, procedures and controls and implementation of these, and the training and competency of the Licensee’s staff. In Great Britain, all consumer-facing land-based gambling businesses must participate in a multi-operator self-exclusion scheme, a consumer-protection measure allowing people who feel they are struggling with their gambling to self-exclude from one or more premises in their area. Despite being made aware of its obligation to participate in a multi-operator self-exclusion scheme, the operator did not do so until the Commission suspended its licence in October 2025. John Pierce, Director of Enforcement and Intelligence, said: “Self-exclusion schemes provide a crucial service for people who feel they are suffering gambling harm. It is important that all operators fully integrate with the scheme and maintain effective safeguards for self-excluded customers. “Every operator must ensure that they are fully participating in a recognised multi-operator self-exclusion scheme, that they have effective procedures to identify and prevent self-excluded customers from gambling in any of their premises, and that their staff are trained to manage self-exclusion and direct individuals to relevant support services. “These are not optional requirements. They are fundamental licence conditions designed to protect consumers from harm, and operators that fail to meet them can expect regulatory action.” Read Holland Park Leisure Limited full penalty . Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement QuinnBet (Gibraltar) Limited to pay £609,104 for regulatory failures 20 August 2026 An online gambling business is to pay £609,104 after a Commission investigation revealed anti-money laundering and social responsibility failures. QuinnBet (Gibraltar) Limited – which runs quinnbet.com – will pay the money as part of a settlement with the Commission. An investigation was launched after a compliance assessment revealed anti-money laundering and social responsibility failures. Social responsibility failures included: deploying a manual process which allowed those aged between 18 to 24 to spend over deposit limits the operator had set for this potentially vulnerable group ineffective controls meant signs of potential gambling harm such as high deposits, short high velocity sessions, increasing stakes, number of bets and high turnover were not captured and flagged for manual review – in one example one customer was able to place approximately 4,800 bets in one day, and 7,000 the following day without this being identified and flagged ineffective controls did not always flag indicators of risk of harm in a timely manner for manual intervention or automated processes – following a large win, one customer’s stakes escalated to the point where over £215,000 was staked in a day with multiple wagers over £5,000 but this was not identified until a report was produced the following day not effectively ensuring all customers who met the relevant threshold underwent a light touch financial vulnerability check . Anti-Money Laundering (AML) failures included: employing insufficient controls to act in a timely manner to identify and mitigate the risk posed by customers who were displaying disproportionate spend – in one example a customer provided payslips that showed monthly earnings of circa £2,000 yet was able to deposit and lose £9,000 in four days allowing some customers to deposit significant funds without the Source of Funds (SoF) being established to evidence that the monies were from a legitimate source having insufficient controls to ensure that Suspicious Activity Reports were submitted as soon as practicable after the threshold for suspicion had been met. John Pierce, Commission Director of Enforcement, said: “This case highlights the serious consequences of relying on systems and controls that are unable to identify and respond to indicators of harm and financial crime quickly enough. We expect operators to ensure their safeguards are effective in practice to protect consumers and keep crime out of gambling. “In this case, the operator recognised the issues and took immediate action to make significant improvements to its systems and controls. This included strengthening their AML policies and procedures and improving how they identify and respond to indicators of harm. “We expect operators to learn from this case and read the public statement to ensure that they do not make the same mistakes. Our key focus is on ensuring that operators meet the standards we expect and, where they fall short, we will take regulatory action where necessary.” Public statements QuinnBet (Gibraltar) Limited Public Statement Published: 20 August 2026 Read the public statement about quinnbet (gibraltar) limited public statement Last updated: 20 August 2026 Show updates to this content No changes to show. The 2024 General Election date of 4 July 2024 was announced to the public by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak on 22 May 2024. In advance of this announcement there was significant planning for a 4 July 2024 General Election. Planning happened at 10 Downing Street and amongst staff at Conservative Campaign Headquarters. Before the date of the General Election was announced, various gambling operators offered special markets in the lead up to the election announcement as to when the General Election would be held. Laura Lee was Head of International for the Conservative Party and the Conservative candidate for Bristol North-West at the 2024 General Election. Laura Lee placed bets on the 2024 General Election with the benefit of confidential information passed to her by her husband about when that election would be called. Anthony Lee, Laura Lee and Amy Hind are due to be sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on 23 October 2026. Craig Williams pleaded Guilty on 29th June and will be sentenced at a later date. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Industry Commission releases gambling industry statistics for 2025 to 2026 17 September 2026 The Gambling Commission has today published its Industry Statistics annual report for the financial year April 2025 to March 2026. The statistics show the customer-facing gambling industry in Great Britain generated a total Gross Gambling Yield (GGY) of £17.5 billion, a 4.4 percent increase on the previous financial year (April 2024 to March 2025). Alongside the annual report , the Commission is also publishing quarterly industry statistics for Quarter 4 (January to March 2026) and the latest wave of data from the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB) . Key facts from annual industry statistics: total GGY (including all reported lotteries): £17.5 billion, 4.4 percent increase on April 2024 to March 2025) total GGY (excluding all reported lotteries): £13.2 billion, 4.7 percent increase total licensed gambling premises in Great Britain: 8,081, 2.0 percent decrease total betting shops in Great Britain: 5,617, 3.6 percent decrease Remote Casino, Betting and Bingo (RCBB) sector GGY: £8.3 billion, 6.9 percent increase land-based sectors GGY (arcades, betting, bingo, casino): £4.9 billion, 1.1 percent increase. Ben Haden, Director of Research and Policy, Gambling Commission, said: “The market shifts that we see in industry data trends, and this year is no different, are complex and will be down to a mix of factors that need more than one source to unpick. "I welcome our capacity to publish industry data alongside the Gambling Survey for Great Britain to encourage and assist in the consideration of key questions from these different perspectives.” Note to editors this report provides an overview of Gross Gambling Yield (GGY) made by licensed gambling operators from GB gambling customers for each customer-facing sector, along with the numbers of licensed operators and premises. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Four arrests and £20,000 seized in illegal gambling raids 23 September 2026 The Gambling Commission and Manchester City Council’s Licensing Team supported Greater Manchester Police during raids on four properties this week. Officers seized mobile phones and gambling-related items including gambling tables, records and account books as part of the operation in Manchester City Centre on Monday night. More that £20,000 in cash was also recovered under the Proceeds of Crime Act. Four people were arrested – two women were arrested on suspicion of immigration offences, one man was arrested on suspicion of running a late-night takeaway without a licence, and one man was arrested on suspicion of money laundering and breaching the Gambling Act. Sue Young, Gambling Commission Executive Director of Operations, said: "Unlicensed operators often have links to wider criminal activity, exploit vulnerable people and undermine legitimate regulated businesses. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Industry New machine rules to support consumers and operators to reduce harm 30 September 2026 New standards to make gaming machines fairer and safer for consumers are to be introduced. Changes include: new category B gaming machines must provide consumers with improved access to gambling management tools and sessional information detailing how long they have been playing for and how much they have won or lost sessional information will be available to licensees to support them in meeting regulatory obligations such as interacting with consumers who are displaying signs of gambling harm improvements in responsible game design by ensuring awards below the stake size are not celebrated and prohibiting features that permit a customer to reduce the time until a result is known. The new changes follow a consultation to implement proposals from the 2023 Gambling Act Review White Paper High stakes: gambling reform for the digital age (opens in new tab) . During the consultation process the Commission considered the evidence provided and made changes to the original proposals to take account of practical and technical considerations and reduce the risk of unintended consequences. Existing gaming machines will be exempt from the new requirements due to the complex technical changes and costs to business that would not necessarily deliver proportionate consumer benefits. In addition, steps have been taken to reduce the risk of consumer and staff ‘alert fatigue’ and to protect consumer privacy. There will be a staged implementation with the bulk of the changes coming into effect in June 2027. Helen Rhodes, Director of Major Policy Projects and Evaluation, said: “These measures will help both to empower consumers to understand and manage their gambling and ensure operators play their part. “Consultation feedback from a range of stakeholders helped to inform our thinking and where there was legitimate and evidenced concern, we made changes. We are confident that the consultation has led to a package of changes where the benefits to consumers are proportionate to the costs of implementation and that the staged timeline for implementation is reasonable and achievable." Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Speeches Allwyn Participant Protection Conference - Sarah Gardner speech 02 October 2026 This speech was delivered by Acting Chief Executive Sarah Gardner at the Allwyn Participant Protection Conference on Thursday 1 October 2026. Please note: This is the speech as drafted and may slightly differ from the delivered version. Thank you everyone and thank you for that introduction. My name is Sarah Gardner and I am currently the Acting Chief Executive of the Gambling Commission, normally the Deputy Chief Executive. Stepping up again this year to be Acting Chief Executive of course brings different challenges and opportunities and I’m delighted to say, joining you all here today for the second Participant Protection Conference is definitely one of the opportunities! Ever since I heard about Allwyn’s commitment to hold these events each year, I’ve been looking forward to the opportunity to attend one and so seeing everyone here today, and looking over the agenda, I’m really pleased to see that commitment fully fledged in reality. Somebody else who I know is pleased to be here today and working on The National Lottery overall is of course the new Interim Chief Executive at Allwyn, Phil Walker. Phil, I’m looking forward to working with you in your new role. I also want to put on record again my thanks to Andria Vidler, the previous Chief Executive of Allwyn. For all the challenges that were encountered, Andria was always committed to transparent and collaborative engagement with me and with the Commission as a whole – a view I know Phil also has. I wish her well for the future. And the future is very much what I want to talk about today. As I have already said, this event is an example of turning commitments into reality but it’s more than that: it is delivering progress. Turning commitments into reality has probably been a theme of the last twelve months for Allwyn as they begin to deliver on their plans to innovate The National Lottery and so I will touch on the achievements delivered so far. But when it comes to participant protection we all want progress too. All of us being here today is strong evidence that progress has been made. But of course, there is always more to do so I will reflect on that as well and how today’s agenda shines a light on how we can all play our part. And I will also talk about why this all matters – why The National Lottery matters. I’ve said it before but The National Lottery is a national institution and so it is on all of us to make sure it stays that way. I mentioned earlier the idea of challenges and opportunities. Protecting and strengthening The National Lottery is clearly both and participant protection runs throughout both the challenge and the opportunity as well. I’ve already said though, plenty of challenges have already been overcome and plenty of commitments have been delivered over the last year, but first, let’s take a moment to reflect on the progress made so far. At the start of this year Allwyn delivered the largest tech upgrade of The National Lottery in its history. This was a crucial moment in the journey of the Fourth Licence and Allwyn’s stewardship of The National Lottery. And the ‘Digital Cutover’ as those of us working on it - and who spent more time thinking about it than was healthy - got used to calling it, was about far more than making sure the tech that supports The National Lottery was upgraded, as important as that was. It was the key gateway to the innovation of products that Allwyn wanted to begin. As the regulator of The National Lottery, the Gambling Commission has played our part, and we are pleased that we have been able to approve a number of new games or game changes. The introduction of Powerball is a clear sign of Allwyn’s ambition to innovate The National Lottery in order to raise Returns to Good Causes and one that we have welcomed. Over the last 12 months where we have published Returns to Good Causes data, The National Lottery has raised £1.7 billion for Good Causes up and down the United Kingdom. The importance of this fundraising cannot be over-estimated. One of the happy parts of my job over the years has been to have the opportunity at times to visit some of the Good Causes that are funded through The National Lottery and see on the ground the benefit delivered. At the Gambling Commission we want to see more of that, of course. So do the Distributors and so do Allwyn. But it’s worth pausing for a minute and thinking about just how transformative that money already is to communities up and down this country. Nothing else in the UK delivers for Good Causes in the same way as The National Lottery does - for our sports clubs, our local museums, our historic sites and much more besides. It matters and so how The National Lottery operates and is perceived matters too. More on that in a moment. Now the figures I just shared will be common knowledge to many of you will here today, but you may be less familiar with other data the Commission collects. Through our official statistics, the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB), we track the participation rates for all products we regulate, including the National Lottery. And the National Lottery is by far and away the product that people participate in when you look at those stats. In the GSGB Annual Report for 2025 that we published in the Summer, the most common gambling activity among all participants was The National Lottery – with 31 per cent of all participants saying they’d played it in the last four weeks. National Lottery scratchcards are played by 11 per cent and National Lottery online instant win games by 6 per cent as well. So the level of engagement with The National Lottery is considerable. Millions of people up and down the country are involved every week, people talk about it, they read about it and their communities are impacted by it. And that impact I talk of is again, the incredible impact of funding Good Causes. There is of course though another impact that can come from any gambling product and that is why today is so important. That impact is of course gambling harms. Now consistently, as shown by the GSGB I was talking about a moment ago, The National Lottery is shown to be one of the lowest risk gambling products anyone can play. But that doesn't mean risks don’t exist and that protections aren’t needed. They are. And that brings me back to the important work Allwyn delivered earlier this year when they delivered that digital transformation of The National Lottery. As part of that, Allwyn have successfully embedded new protections for every single player of The National Lottery who plays online or through the App. And Allwyn are also committed to working hard with retailers up and down the country to strengthen support for players at risk of harm in retail as well. This work to strengthen participant protection was an important commitment by Allwyn to the future of The National Lottery and it is great to see that commitment now being delivered and progressing. That’s not to say such changes happen seamlessly. There have been teething issues - we all know sometimes a step forward might be followed by a step back – but the commitment, and the progress that has followed so far, to player protection is real and is something that I and the Commission fully support.…

Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Two men sentenced after operating an illegal gambling den 05 October 2026 Two men have been given suspended prison sentences for possessing and transferring criminal funds obtained through the running of illegal poker games in Cardiff. Between August 2022 and February 2024, Noor Rassam and Panayiotis Karayiannis ran illegal poker games from an upstairs room within a unit on an industrial estate in Splott. The premises had been fitted out with six poker tables, a spinning prize wheel, seating areas, and fridges stocked with drinks and snacks. In February 2024, officers from Tarian, the Regional Organised Crime Unit (ROCU) working alongside the Gambling Commission, HMRC and Cardiff Council’s Licensing Department, executed warrants at the industrial unit, as well as residential and business addresses linked to the two men. Rassam, 29, from Pentwyn, Cardiff, and Karayiannis, 30, from Pontprennau, Cardiff, were sentenced to three years in prison, suspended for three years. Both men admitted to possessing criminal property, contrary to the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and transferring criminal property, contrary to the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. A Proceeds of Crime Act hearing has been set for the 9 April 2027. Sue Young, Gambling Commission Executive Director of Operations, said: “This case emerged after we received information about an illegal gambling den. The message is clear – if you run an illegal casino, there will be a tip off, you will be caught, and there will be significant consequences. “We will continue to work with partners and take action against those who run illegal gambling operations in Great Britain.” Detective Constable Charles Lan, of Tarian ROCU, said: “These two men operated an illegal gambling business for their own financial gain, generating substantial profits which were never declared for tax purposes and ultimately came at the expense of the wider public. “Their criminal enterprise provided them with significant personal benefits, funding a lavish lifestyle that included foreign holidays and other high-value spending. “Throughout the investigation, we uncovered evidence that they actively promoted their poker games to individuals involved in serious criminality and even boasted about the presence of drug dealers and organised crime group members at their events. By providing a venue for these individuals and profiting from their participation, they were helping to facilitate and fund further criminal activity. “The harm caused by this operation should not be underestimated. Individuals lost significant sums of money through these games, with some becoming indebted to the organisers. Unlike legitimate gambling operators, there were no safeguards in place to identify or support vulnerable people, nor any measures to protect those experiencing gambling addiction. “This sentence sends a message that unlicensed gambling is not a victimless offence. Those who seek to profit from illegal gambling while ignoring the laws and protections designed to keep people safe can expect to be brought before the courts. “I would like to thank our partners, particularly the Gambling Commission, whose intelligence first brought this activity to our attention. Their expertise and support throughout the investigation were instrumental in bringing this case to a successful conclusion. I would also like to thank HMRC and Cardiff Council’s Licensing Department for their valued assistance.” Read full story on the Tarian Regional Organised Crime Unit website Last updated: 5 October 2026 Show updates to this content No changes to show. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Land-based casino operators to pay £5m for regulatory failures 07 October 2026 Three nation-wide casino operators are to pay £5 million after a Gambling Commission investigation revealed anti-money laundering and social responsibility failures. Rank Group PLC owned operators Grosvenor Casinos Limited, Grosvenor Casinos (GC) Limited and Gaming Group Limited - who run 51 casinos across Great Britain - will also undergo a third-party audit to ensure they are effectively implementing anti-money laundering and safer gambling policies, procedures and controls. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) failures included: not updating its AML policies to take account of changes to the Money Laundering Regulations in 2020 implementing AML policies, procedures and controls which allowed inconsistent decisions to be applied to customers with elevated money laundering risk implementing unclear policies, procedures and controls which resulted in inappropriate risk levels being ascribed to high-risk customers and high-risk sources of funds being used by customers without appropriate scrutiny not carrying out enhanced customer due diligence checks when its own policies required it. Social responsibility failures included: not carrying out safer gambling interactions with a customer during a period in which they lost £50,000 not having a record of any safer gambling interactions with a customer who won approximately £260,000 in a short period and then lost around £250,000 in 12 days not carrying out safer gambling interactions with a customer, who was returning after a period of self-exclusion, until they had lost £25,000. All £5 million of the settlement will be directed to the Government’s Consolidated Fund. Sue Young, Executive Director of Operations, said: "Larger enforcement cases are often associated with online gambling but, as today’s announcement shows, the risks of anti-money laundering and social responsibility failures are equally alive in the land-based sector. “We would advise all premises-based operators to take a careful look at this case and ensure their own business is not making the same mistakes, and therefore they do not face costly and inevitable Commission action.” Public statements Grosvenor Casinos Limited Public Statement Published: 7 October 2026 Read the public statement about grosvenor casinos limited public statement Last updated: 7 October 2026 Show updates to this content No changes to show. Please note: This is the speech as drafted and may slightly differ from the delivered version. Hello everyone, thank you for that warm welcome. My name is Sarah Gardner and I am Acting Chief Executive, normally Deputy Chief Exec, of the Gambling Commission back home in Great Britain (GB). And thank you to the outgoing President, Ben Haden for that kind introduction as well. Of course, he has to be kind as he works with me back in Great Britain and it’s a long flight back from Peru! And being here in the historic city of Lima this week, I should also say ‘buenas tardes’ to our hosts and to all of you from Latin America. One of the great things about IAGR is being able to meet so many colleagues from around the world all in the same place, to share the issues that we are working on and – regardless of the language we speak – to know you are speaking to those who have the same worries and the same aims. More on that later but for now ‘muchas gracias’ to our Peruvian hosts. And with that I promise not to push my Spanish and your patience further! Today I’m going to speak about some things we are doing in GB and share learning I believe could be useful on an international basis. My comments will include our effort to tackle the illegal market and how we play our part in a transformed research space. On that note, I’m going to talk about some new research we are publishing today on illegal gambling. Much of what I will say will overlap themes from other speeches and panellists which are insightful. The common issues amongst you and value of IAGR bringing us together like this. But first, to provide a bit of context to all of this, let’s have a little look at where things stand in Great Britain today. If we look at the data we collect, the year ending in March 2026 appears another year of growth. For the whole regulated sector across Great Britain, Gross Gambling Yield (GGY) was up to £17.5 billion – a 4.4 per cent increase on the year before. If we take all lotteries out of the equation GGY is £13.2 billion – up by 4.7 per cent on the year before. And whilst we’re on lotteries, whilst the core products remain distinct, and for us how we regulate our National Lottery is under different laws, it is increasingly true that the lottery sector is blurring into the commercial gambling sector, whether through ownership or other avenues. This is a trend we are paying attention to. But back to the stats. If we drill down again, GGY for ‘remote’ betting, casino and bingo, for which the vast majority is online, was £8.3 billion – a 6.9 per cent increase on the year before. When we factor this in against the picture from the Gambling Survey for Great Britain, we know 47 per cent of those surveyed, aged 18 and over, participated in gambling in the past 4 weeks. Again, when we exclude people who only play lottery draws, participation was 27 per cent. The population of Great Britain population is currently over 67 million people, so that’s tens of millions of people engaged in some form of gambling every month. These participation rates are stable with the year before and have been stable for a long time. And again, if you look back at previous years since the pandemic, the story is familiar – steady growth in GGY from a stable and sizeable player base. It gives the impression that consumers, operators and we as the regulator are stood on solid ground in Great Britain – the solid ground of a mature, developed market. But impressions can be misleading. This picture follows several years of strengthening gambling regulation and raising standards of compliance with our rules. The UK Government has made important changes and interventions that impact the gambling sector as well in that time. And at the Gambling Commission things have changed. And change is an important point when we look at the debate in Great Britain at present. Before I move on, as I mention change at the Commission, many of you will know that we have seen some people changes over recent months. I was delighted to welcome Ruth Evans just a couple of weeks ago as the new Chair of the Commission, Ruth having been appointed by the UK Government for a five year term. I am very much looking forward to working with her and I take this opportunity to place on record our thanks to Charles Counsell for stepping in as Interim Chair. We have also seen some change in our Executive team. After ten years with the Commission, Tim Miller announced earlier this year that he would pursue a change. Tim is well known to many of you here so I would like to take the opportunity to thank him for his service to the Commission and to wish him well. I was delighted to welcome Sarah Fox to the Commission last month to take over much of Tim’s portfolio, alongside regulation of the National Lottery. Sarah is no stranger to gambling, having come from leading the Gambling team in the UK Government, so has been able to hit the ground running. The fact that I am speaking to you today as Acting CEO is also a reminder that the Commission will soon welcome a new Chief Executive. I just want to mention here, and not only because he is in the room in a hall full of so many of his friends and colleagues over the years, my thanks again for everything Andrew Rhodes did in his time at the Gambling Commission. He was a great colleague and, backed up by the great team at the Commission more widely, he made an important impact to our work and the sector as a whole. As I say, we are now working on recruiting Andrew’s successor and we will of course keep you all updated on that as we progress and I know that meeting colleagues across the IAGR community will be a priority for an incoming CEO. Back to the wider picture though and last year the UK Government made changes to the way gambling is taxed across Great Britain, many of which were to begin in April this year – so just after the period covered by the stats I just gave you. Now the Gambling Commission does not play any role in setting gambling tax rates, collecting those gambling taxes or even advising on tax. However, we do have a statutory role to advise ministers on gambling and its regulation so it is important that we monitor and understand the impact of things like taxation on the industry we regulate. In the case of these most recent changes which were announced by the Government in their Budget last November, the full impact is not yet clear as it’s really too early for that. The industry is working through the implications and at the Commission we continue to engage with those we regulate to understand their position. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement L & L Europe pays £900,000 for failures including withdrawal delays 21 October 2026 An online gambling business is to pay £900,000 for regulatory failures, including unnecessarily delaying consumer withdrawals. L & L Europe Limited - which runs seven websites including allbritishcasino.com, casinocasino.com and hypercasino.com - will pay the money as part of a regulatory settlement with the Commission. Withdrawal-related failures included: employing a term and condition which stated customers were only permitted to request one withdrawal at a time and could not request a further withdrawal until the original one l had been authorised – this is unfair within the meaning of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 manually reviewing every fifth or tenth withdrawal for some customers led to customers being required to provide additional information prior to withdrawals being processed – Commission requirements state that a request by a customer to withdraw funds from their account must not result in a requirement for additional information to be supplied as a condition of withdrawal if the licensee could have reasonably requested that information earlier. The Commission’s investigation also revealed anti-money laundering and social responsibility failings. Anti-money laundering failures included: controls in place to identify risks associated with money laundering and terrorist financing were not appropriate as they were largely based on financial thresholds and sampling at set thresholds, rather than based on risk factors and customer risk profiles not following its own customer due diligence procedures including not considering the risks posed by newly-opened bank accounts or money in bank accounts not being evidenced as coming from employment, a business income or savings. Social responsibility failings included: safer gambling alerts flagging potential gambling harm such as time spent gambling or failed deposits were activated in respect of some websites but not across the Licensee’s entire suite of websites not having a process in place to evaluate the effectiveness of its overall approach to customer interaction. Sue Young, Executive Director of Operations, said: “As a regulator we expect consumers to be treated fairly. “A basic expectation is that when you have winnings you can withdraw those swiftly without hinderance from unfair terms and conditions or the operator failing to carry out checks at an earlier stage. That is essential to consumer trust. “There may be occasions where a gambling business can ask consumers for information at withdrawal to fulfil legal obligations, but this was not the case here. “We hope this case sends a clear reminder to the industry that, although much of our enforcement action frequently relates to anti-money laundering and social responsibility failings, we will not hesitate to act when we see incidents of gambling not being fair and open.” Public statements L & L Europe Limited Public Statement Published: 21 October 2026 Read the public statement about l & l europe limited public statement Last updated: 21 October 2026 Show updates to this content No changes to show. Hide Cookie Message Skip to main content Home News Enforcement Three sentenced for General Election betting offences 23 October 2026 Three people have been sentenced for offences of cheating relating to bets placed on the date of the 2024 General Election. Anthony Lee, Laura Lee and Amy Hind appeared at Southwark Crown Court today (23 October 2026) having previously pleaded guilty to offences under section 42 of the Gambling Act 2005. Anthony Lee received a custodial sentence of 10 months and 2 weeks imprisonment on each count to be served concurrently (Suspended for 12 months), 100 hours unpaid work to be completed in the next the 12 months; Laura Lee received a custodial sentence of 4 months and 2 weeks imprisonment (Suspended for 12 months), 40 hours unpaid work to be completed in the next 12 months; Amy Hind received a custodial sentence of 6 months imprisonment (Suspended for 12 months), 50 hours unpaid work to be completed in the next 12 months. All defendants are subject to a probation requirement for the next 12 months and all defendants have a prohibited activity requirement for the next 12 months from using online gambling applications. Katharine Diamond, General Counsel at the Gambling Commission, said: "I’d like to thank colleagues across the Gambling Commission, particularly in our intelligence, enforcement, counsel and legal teams, for their hard work in bringing this case to this point. "This is a significant case and a first of its kind for the Commission, demonstrating our commitment to protecting the integrity of betting markets. “Betting markets must be fair and must not be undermined by people using confidential information for their own benefit. “These convictions demonstrate the importance of protecting the integrity of gambling markets and acting where there is evidence that individuals have sought to cheat. “We will continue to investigate suspected criminal activity and use our powers to protect the integrity of gambling.” Anthony Lee and Laura Lee are to pay £1,000 each prosecution costs. No order for costs was made in respect of Amy Hind. The court heard that the date of the 2024 General Election was announced by then Prime Minister Rishi Sunak on 22 May 2024. Before the announcement, there had been significant planning for an election to be held on 4 July, including discussions at 10 Downing Street and among staff at Conservative Campaign Headquarters. In the period before the announcement, gambling operators offered markets on when the General Election would be held. Anthony Lee was the Conservative Party's Director of Campaigning and, through his role, was party to confidential discussions about the timing of the General Election. He used that information to place bets and passed the information to his wife, Laura Lee. Laura Lee, who was Head of International for the Conservative Party and a Conservative candidate at the 2024 General Election, placed bets on the election date using confidential information passed to her by her husband. Amy Hind, who had previously worked for the Conservative Party and was working for the NHS at the time, placed bets after receiving confidential information about when the General Election would be called. The Commission has previously announced that Craig Williams pleaded guilty to an offence of cheating in relation to betting on the date of the 2024 General Election. He will be sentenced at a later date. Simon Chatfield, Paul Place, Iain Makepeace, James Ward, Thomas James, Russell George, Charlotte Lang, Jacob Willmer, Jeremy Hunt and Nick Mason are also charged with offences of cheating relating to bets placed on the date of the 2024 General Election and they are due to stand trial in September 2027 and January 2028. title: MGA Concludes Consultation on Proposed Updates to Recognition Notice Framework
excerpt: MGA Concludes Consultation on Proposed Updates to Recognition Notice Framework - Malta Gaming Authority The Malta Gaming Authority has completed its review of feedback submitted during the targeted consultation on proposed updates to the Recognition Notice (RN) Framework and thanks all stakeholders who participated and shared their views. The consultation offered a valuable opportunity to consider the proposed approach and its practical application. The feedback received informed a number of refinements to ensure that the revised approach remains proportionate, risk-based and practical for RN holders. A Feedback Statement summarising the feedback received, the Authority’s position and the way forward has been circulated to RN holders and their representatives. The Authority will share further information on the practical application of specific requirements in due course.
